name: Yaeba (fang tooth look)

lead: Yaeba (八重歯, "double tooth") describes upper canines that sit high or overlap neighboring teeth, giving a fang-like smile. In Japan some people see it as a sign of youth and natural beauty.

For people who want the look, the appeal is a softer, younger-looking smile. Those without it can get tsuke-yaeba, attachable false teeth, and in the early 2010s some teenage girls had canines capped with crowns. A 2023 web survey found Japanese respondents rated crowded front teeth higher than US respondents did.

paras: The least permanent route is removable attachments that clip over the canines, offered by some Tokyo clinics from about 2012. A more permanent route, capping, was reported in the early 2010s. The trend centered on young women and was linked to idols.

Crowns or reshaping alter healthy teeth permanently and can affect bite and cleaning. Crowded teeth are also harder to keep clean, and demand for orthodontic straightening is reported to be growing. Dentists should be consulted before any irreversible change.

angle.text: Those who want the look add attachable false canines or caps so the smile shows prominent canine teeth that some viewers find cute and youthful. Natural yaeba already produces the same visual effect.

lead: Yaeba (八重歯, "double tooth") is a Japanese term for teeth, usually upper canines, that look unusually fang-like, most often because they overlap a neighbor or sit higher in the gum.[1] In Japan the look is described as a sign of youthfulness and natural beauty.[1]

The trend is said to have started in 2011 with the AKB48 singer and actress Tomomi Itano, who popularized the look with a false tooth.[1] In the early 2010s many teenage girls had canines capped to create it.[1] A parody group named TYB48, launched in 2011 and active for about two years, had members who all had yaeba and was created to promote a dental clinic.[1] People who want the look use attachable false canines (tsuke-yaeba), which Tokyo clinics such as one in Ginza were reported to offer from around 2012.[2]

paras: The look involves an upper canine that overlaps a lateral incisor or sits above the line of its neighbors.[1][2] The word appears in Japanese texts from the late Edo period and is distinguished from "kiba", which refers to fangs or sharp canines.[2]

The 2011 trend was tied to Tomomi Itano of AKB48, and the group TYB48 spread it as a parody and clinic promotion.[1] Coverage cited in Wikipedia includes a 2012 book and 2013 and 2018 news pieces.[1] One account says the vogue peaked in the mid-2010s and is now much less common, with demand for orthodontics growing.[2]

The off-the-shelf version is removable false teeth or ceramic attachments sold at some Tokyo dental clinics, with reported prices of tens of thousands of yen, including crystal-embellished versions.[2] Capping natural canines with crowns, reported in the early 2010s, is a permanent change.[1]

A 2023 web survey of 200 respondents, as summarized in one account, reported higher attractiveness ratings for images with maxillary anterior crowding from Japanese respondents than from US respondents.[2] The figures come from that summary and should be checked against the original study.
No studies found. Survey research on perceptions of crowded canines is summarized above.

timeline.event: Trend linked to Tomomi Itano; TYB48 launched.[1]
Attachable yaeba offered by Tokyo clinics.[2]
TYB48 ends after about two years.[1]
